title: Simultaneous spike-resolved recording from every neuron in one behaving mammalian brain

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to record when every neuron fires an action potential, simultaneously, throughout one mammalian brain while the animal behaves. Each spike must be assigned to its originating neuron, so the result is a set of neuron-identified spike trains spanning the same behavioral events. Whole-brain coverage, reliable neuron identity, spike timing and simultaneity are separate requirements; achieving some does not establish the others.

Existing approaches documented here capture different parts of this goal. Electrophysiology measures spikes from sampled neurons. Pooling recordings across animals expands anatomical coverage but cannot recover the simultaneous activity of one complete brain. Calcium imaging measures fluorescence associated with neuronal calcium, with temporal resolution constrained by indicator kinetics and acquisition rate. It can inform spike inference, but a large calcium-imaged population is not automatically a population with individually validated spike times.

significance.text: If achieved, this would transform the observation of distributed brain activity: researchers could follow spiking across the entire brain during the same individual perception, decision or movement. Relationships between distant populations would no longer have to be reconstructed solely from separate sampled recordings or different animals. The immediate advance would be a comprehensive measurement of brain-wide spiking during behavior, providing a stronger empirical basis for studying coordinated population dynamics.

The scale is substantial even in a mouse. Herculano-Houzel, Mota and Lent reported an estimated total of 70.89 ± 10.41 million mouse-brain neurons in their 2006 study. This is a biological scale estimate, not an exact census for every mouse or a demonstrated recording capacity. By comparison, the documented million-neuron optical demonstration sampled a cortical volume approximately 0.5 mm thick and measured calcium fluorescence.

A complete set of spike trains would still measure a specific variable: action-potential event times attributed to neurons. It would not capture every electrical variable, all synaptic or molecular states, or the peripheral nervous system. Simultaneous observation alone would not establish causal mechanisms or provide the ability to control the recorded activity.

Conditional synthesis: such recordings could support stronger tests of circuit theories, constrain simulations and reveal where sampled measurements miss behaviorally relevant dynamics. Those outcomes would also require suitable models, complementary measurements and, for causal claims, interventions. The recording capability alone would not provide a sufficient specification for a faithful brain simulation. Its feasibility and time to completion remain uncertain; the supplied evidence does not justify a forecast that it will take decades.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is to combine complete anatomical coverage with simultaneous, neuron-identified spike measurement in one behaving mammal. Sampling neurons across many regions is insufficient if substantial populations remain unobserved, and assembling a brain-wide map across animals cannot substitute for recording all populations during the same events. The supplied demonstrations establish progress toward components of this capability, without demonstrating their conjunction.

Physical access and measurement throughput are major engineering barriers. An optical approach must collect separable signals throughout scattering tissue, including deep structures, while acquiring them fast enough for the intended spike-timing accuracy. Scaling parallel optical measurements also raises power and tissue-heating concerns: the light-beads microscopy supplement explicitly analyzes the increased optical power required as measurement multiplicity grows. The demonstrated 0.5 mm axial extent describes that experiment's coverage, not a universal depth limit for all optical methods.

Signal separation and validation are equally fundamental. A system must distinguish neurons whose signals overlap, avoid splitting one neuron's activity into several apparent units, avoid merging several neurons into one unit, and detect spikes with independently assessed timing accuracy. It must also establish which neurons are present but silent during the recording. The light-beads supplement's simulation-based estimate of detecting approximately 80% of active cells within the volumetric field illustrates why detecting many cells and proving complete neuronal coverage are different achievements.

Engineering synthesis: the complete system would need to sustain acquisition, signal processing and data handling across the brain while preserving behavior and limiting measurement-induced tissue effects. Increasing channel count alone would not solve anatomical access, neuron identification, temporal fidelity or biological disturbance. The supplied record does not establish a single architecture that resolves these constraints together.

current_state.text: A review by J. H. Siegle and N. A. Steinmetz, published on 1 May 2026 in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, reports that large-scale electrophysiology routinely captures spike trains from thousands of neurons distributed across the brain. This supports the scale of routine sampled recordings; it does not establish a hard upper limit on exceptional experiments. The supplied review retained the abstract and glossary, while the main review was unavailable in the subscription preview.

The International Brain Laboratory's 2025 Nature study assembled a brain-wide electrophysiological map using 699 Neuropixels probe insertions across 139 mice in 12 laboratories. Although the abstract describes 621,733 neurons, the retained main text specifies 621,733 units including multineuron activity, with 75,708 classified as well-isolated neurons after quality control. The insertions were distributed across an entire hemisphere, and recordings mostly used two simultaneous probes. These are pooled measurements across animals, rather than simultaneous whole-brain coverage in one animal. The supplied evidence does not establish a ranking of this map as the strongest available.

Demas and colleagues reported in Nature Methods in 2021 that light-beads microscopy recorded populations of approximately one million mouse cortical neurons in volumes of about 5.4 × 6 × 0.5 mm at approximately 2 Hz. The retained figure caption identifies the calcium indicator GCaMP6s, and the supplement specifies bilateral cortical regions and an acquisition rate of 2.2 Hz for the bi-hemispheric configuration. These measurements provide extensive cortical calcium activity, rather than validated spike times from every neuron throughout the brain.

The light-beads main article was available only in part, but its supplementary information was retained in full. Supplementary simulations estimated extraction of the majority, approximately 80%, of active cells within the volumetric field of view. That estimate concerns active-cell extraction under the modeled conditions; it is neither an independent census of all neurons nor evidence of whole-brain coverage. It also should not be converted into an exact correction to the headline population count.

Unresolved comparison from the research notes: a larval-zebrafish study dated 11 July 2025 was described as recording approximately half of the neuronal population at that developmental stage using calcium signals. The supplied evidence review did not substantiate the fraction, transparency or signal comparison from retained source passages. This comparison therefore remains unverified here; that evidence limitation does not establish that the reported result is false.

Evidence scope: the documented 2021, 2025 and May 2026 results do not demonstrate the proposed capability, but the supplied material does not establish an exhaustive search through 1 November 2026. The IBL article extraction was truncated after the relevant retained sections. Missing figure images and effectively blank reporting-summary extractions provide no additional evidence. These access limits bound the conclusions without negating the dated findings described above.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: record neuron-identified spikes simultaneously throughout one mouse or larger mammalian brain for at least several minutes while the animal performs a skilled sensory-motor behavior. Coverage should include both hemispheres, cerebellum, brainstem and other subcortical structures. Duration and task choice are proposed practical requirements, not established standards, and the reported achievement should state the species, preparation, behavior and recording conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Simultaneous whole-brain neuron-identified spikes for several minutes during skilled behavior

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: establish neuronal coverage independently of the recorded activity, including neurons that remain silent during the session. Prespecify tolerances and report missed neurons, missed spikes, false spike detections, false splits, false merges and timing errors. Independent checks of true spike times and neuron identities are grounded in the review's description of recording ground truth; the supplied sources do not prescribe numerical acceptance thresholds for this whole-brain goal.
completion_criteria.label: Activity-independent neuronal coverage and recording fidelity validated against ground truth

completion_criteria.text: Proposed robustness check: show that prespecified population analyses remain stable when uncertain recorded units are excluded, and assess whether omissions are concentrated in particular regions or populations. This supplements independent coverage validation. Removing uncertain recorded units cannot reveal neurons that were never observed, and stable analyses can still tolerate systematic omissions. Large detected populations likewise do not establish complete extraction, as illustrated by the light-beads supplement's active-cell detection analysis.
completion_criteria.label: Population analyses remain stable after excluding uncertain recorded units

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the result in a second session or animal, with independent replication providing stronger evidence of transferability. Report measurement-related tissue effects, behavioral performance, usable duration and the anatomical scope over which accuracy was validated. Finite demonstrations establish performance and breadth under tested conditions; they do not establish applicability to every mammalian species, brain state or behavior. Any claim of every-neuron coverage must state the remaining uncertainty in the neuronal census and recording fidelity.
completion_criteria.label: Recording reproduced with practical limits and remaining coverage uncertainty reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NEU-02, routine synaptic-resolution connectomics of entire mammalian brains, concerns anatomical wiring; NEU-01 concerns activity over time. They could provide complementary structural and functional measurements without either guaranteeing the other. NEU-03, a prospective theory predicting mammalian circuit computation from connectivity, concerns explanatory and predictive capability. NEU-01 could supply demanding activity data for testing such a theory, but comprehensive recording would not itself constitute that theory.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-07 requires noninvasive cellular-resolution reading and writing through the intact adult human skull. NEU-01 permits a mouse or another mammal and does not require noninvasiveness, an intact skull or writing activity. NEU-09 concerns cell-type-specific molecular access throughout the intact adult human brain. Molecular access could help enable some recording strategies, but access alone does not provide simultaneous neuron-identified spike trains.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-04 concerns content-faithful reading and writing of specific episodic memories, which requires identifying and manipulating memory content beyond recording spikes. NEU-10 seeks a causal, measurement-grade account of conscious content, adding causal explanation and content attribution. NEU-12 seeks an account of sleep sufficient to complete its necessary brain functions without a normal sleep period. NEU-01 could inform each research program, but observation alone would not meet their distinct completion goals.

Roster-based synthesis: NEU-05 concerns target-specific long-axon regrowth in the adult mammalian central nervous system, and NEU-06 concerns reconstructing human cognitive circuits after neuronal loss. NEU-08 concerns a developmental code that builds a specified functional circuit, while NEU-11 concerns reversible, circuit-specific reopening of adult critical-period plasticity. Whole-brain spike recording could help evaluate the functional effects of repair, circuit construction or altered plasticity; it would not itself deliver any of those capabilities. These distinctions follow from the supplied roster titles, whose detailed specifications were not provided.

unresolved_issues: The supplied freshness record does not establish exhaustive coverage through 1 November 2026 or exclude later or omitted demonstrations.
The larval-zebrafish fraction, developmental scope and modality comparison remain unverified from the supplied evidence.
No numerical tolerances or validated whole-brain method for independently accounting for every neuron, including silent neurons, are supplied.
Feasibility, an implementation architecture and time to completion remain unresolved.
The biological and behavioral disturbance acceptable for a convincing demonstration requires a prespecified practical boundary.
Related-concept distinctions are based on supplied titles; their detailed requirements and dependencies remain unspecified.

The review's recommendation to remove the zebrafish assertion was adapted by retaining it only as an unresolved comparison, preserving potentially useful research detail without asserting it as established.
The review's inability to verify NEU-02, NEU-03 and NEU-07 identities is partly resolved by the supplied roster, but the earlier cross-concept dependency claims remain unjustified.

brief.title: Recording every nerve cell firing in a behaving mammal
possible: Researchers could follow every neuron, or nerve cell, in a mammal’s brain as the animal senses, decides and moves. They could record spikes, the cells’ brief electrical pulses, across the whole brain at once and identify which cell fired each pulse.
why: Researchers could see how distant groups of cells coordinate during the same decision or movement. This would help test theories of how brains work and reveal activity that smaller samples miss.

sources.who: Suzana Herculano-Houzel, Bruno Mota and Roberto Lent
sources.showed: They estimated that a mouse brain contains about 71 million neurons and compared how neuron populations grow across rodent species.
sources.quote: In contrast, although the relative cortical size increases with total brain size, the cortical fraction of total brain neurons remains constant.
sources.cited_for: The neuron count illustrates the scale of recording an entire mouse brain.
sources.not_established: A population estimate does not identify every neuron in an individual brain or demonstrate recording capacity.

sources.who: Jeffrey Demas, Alipasha Vaziri and colleagues
sources.showed: Their microscope recorded calcium signals, fluorescent changes associated with cell activity, from about a million neurons in the mouse brain’s outer layer.
sources.quote: Using LBM, we demonstrate mesoscopic and volumetric imaging at multiple scales in the mouse cortex
sources.cited_for: Optical measurements can capture activity across very large cell populations.
sources.not_established: They did not measure independently validated spike times from every neuron throughout the brain.

sources.who: Joshua H. Siegle and Nicholas A. Steinmetz
sources.showed: Their review describes routine recordings of spikes from sampled neurons distributed across the brain.
sources.quote: Recent advances in electrode technology — including the development of Neuropixels and SiNAPS probes — have made it possible to routinely capture spike trains from thousands of neurons distributed across the brain.
sources.cited_for: Electrical recording already measures individual spikes across widely separated brain regions.
sources.not_established: Routine sampled recordings do not establish simultaneous coverage of every neuron.

sources.showed: They assembled a map of electrical activity during decision-making across many mice, including 75,708 neurons whose signals could be individually distinguished.
sources.quote: Neural responses correlated with impending motor action almost everywhere in the brain.
sources.cited_for: A shared behavioral task reveals activity associated with actions across widely distributed brain regions.
sources.not_established: Measurements pooled across animals do not capture a complete brain during the same events.

shown: Electrical recordings routinely capture individual spikes from thousands of neurons across the brain. Demas and colleagues reached much larger populations using calcium imaging, while the International Brain Laboratory mapped activity across many animals. These approaches achieve different parts of the goal.
missing: No demonstration combines complete brain coverage with simultaneous, individually identified spikes in a behaving mammal.
Coverage must account for silent cells, separate overlapping signals and independently establish spike timing and cell identity.
A complete system must reach deep structures and handle the signals while preserving behavior and limiting tissue damage or heating.

milestones.label: Every neuron recorded together during skilled behavior
milestones.explanation: Identified spikes would have to be recorded throughout a behaving mammal’s brain, including both halves and deep structures, for several minutes. This would combine coverage, timing and behavior.

milestones.label: Coverage and accuracy checked against independent measurements
milestones.explanation: Independent checks would have to count silent neurons and quantify missed cells, spike errors, mistaken identities and timing errors against preset limits. This would establish recording completeness and accuracy.

milestones.label: Results withstand removal of uncertain recordings
milestones.explanation: Planned analyses would have to remain stable after uncertain recordings are excluded, with omissions assessed across regions and cell groups. This would test whether uncertain signals distort the conclusions.

milestones.label: Repeated recording with practical limits and uncertainty reported
milestones.explanation: The result would have to recur in another session or animal, with tissue effects, behavior, usable duration, validated coverage and remaining uncertainty reported. This would establish repeatability and practical limits.

uncertain: A method for independently accounting for every neuron, including silent cells, and acceptable error limits remain unresolved.
The acceptable effects on tissue and behavior still need to be defined.
Whether a workable system can combine all the requirements, and how long that would take, remain unknown.

page.title: Whole-brain spike recording from every neuron in a behaving mammal
page.definition: Every action potential, or brief electrical spike, is recorded simultaneously from every neuron in one mammalian brain during behavior. Each spike is assigned to its originating cell.

goal.need: Four adult male Swiss mice contained an estimated 70.89 ± 10.41 million brain neurons (mean ± SD); 59.0 ± 5.0% were in the cerebellum. The Brain Activity Map proposal seeks complete-circuit spike recordings to reconstruct interactions among neuronal populations during behavioral events. Recording cerebral cortex alone leaves most mouse brain neurons unobserved.

completion.title: A validated recording captures every brain neuron's spikes simultaneously during behavior.
completion.criterion: For one mammal during an observed behavioral interval, obtain simultaneous spike trains from every neuron throughout its brain. Assign each action potential to its originating neuron and verify spike timing and identity independently. An activity-independent census must also account for neurons that remain silent. Coverage includes both hemispheres, cerebellum, brainstem and other subcortical structures. The cited sources set no minimum duration or acceptable error rate for this conjunction.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; the cited roadmaps establish component goals but provide no operational acceptance test for their conjunction.
completion.basis: Searches of NIH BRAIN 2025, the Brain Activity Map roadmap, NSF–Kavli workshop recommendations and whole-brain recording standards found no operational acceptance test combining mammalian whole-brain coverage, identified spikes and behavior. The fallback joins the published complete-circuit spike goal to behavioral recording, without adding numerical duration or accuracy cutoffs.

milestones.title: Voltage indicators detect single action potentials in living mammalian neurons.
milestones.criterion: Genetically encoded fluorescent voltage sensors detect individual action potentials in neural populations in vivo, as targeted by NIH. On 12 December 2019, Villette et al. reported paired optical and whole-cell measurements from 8 neurons in 3 anaesthetized mice; 7 cells fired 1,022 spikes. This establishes detection in sampled neurons without establishing complete-population recording.
milestones.set_by: NIH BRAIN Initiative Working Group, BRAIN 2025, Section III.3g-ii, optical-recording milestones.

milestones.title: Optical recordings capture activity from 1–10 million neurons in one behaving mammal.
milestones.criterion: Optical instrumentation records activity from 1–10 million neurons in a behaving mammal. On 30 August 2021, Demas et al. reported 1,065,289 cortical neurons in one mouse, sampled at 2.2 Hz across approximately 5.4 × 6 × 0.5 mm for 9 minutes. GCaMP6s fluorescence reports calcium changes. This reaches the population target's lower end without establishing individual spike times.
milestones.set_by: NIH BRAIN Initiative Working Group, BRAIN 2025, Section III.3g-ii. This population target does not require spike-resolved recording.
milestones.threshold_quote: 1-10 million neuron recordings in behaving mammal.

milestones.title: Every neuron yields an identified spike train simultaneously in one anaesthetized mammalian brain.
milestones.criterion: One living, anaesthetized mammal yields simultaneous, neuron-identified spike trains throughout its entire brain, including both hemispheres, cerebellum, brainstem and other subcortical structures. An activity-independent census accounts for every neuron, including silent neurons; independent measurements validate spike timing and cell identity. This intermediate test removes only the behavioral condition from completion. The cited demonstrations do not satisfy it.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of NIH BRAIN 2025, the Brain Activity Map roadmap and NSF–Kavli recommendations found no published penultimate whole-mammal spike-recording test.

not_found: No whole-brain, all-neuron validation protocol with numerical tolerances for missed neurons, spike errors or timing errors was found.
The main text of the review published on 1 May 2026 was inaccessible; its abstract and glossary were available.

results.finding: Postmortem whole-brain estimates from 4 mice averaged 70.89 million neurons.
results.detail: The activity-independent estimate used sampled nuclei from dissected tissue. It did not identify every neuron or record spike trains in a living brain.

results.finding: Optical recording captured activity from 1,065,289 cortical neurons in one mouse.
results.detail: The million-neuron recording used GCaMP6s at 2.2 Hz. The provided text does not establish that the mouse was behaving during this particular recording; behavior is described for other recordings.
results.quote: Fig. 5: Volumetric recording of 1,065,289 neurons within a volume of ~5.4 × 6 × 0.5 mm at 2.2 Hz in a GCaMP6s-expressing mouse with no external stimulation.

results.finding: In one awake mouse, voltage imaging recorded 182 cortical neurons; 88 showed visually evoked spiking.
results.detail: The genetically encoded indicator JEDI-2P-Kv was used in visual cortex. Spikes were identified from optical voltage traces; the recording did not cover the whole brain.
results.quote: From the spiking activity of the 182 neurons, we identified 88 neurons with visually evoked suprathreshold activity.

results.finding: Mouse cortical voltage imaging simultaneously recorded more than 300 spiking neurons.
results.detail: The recordings were made in vivo, but the supplied text does not identify the voltage indicator used as genetically encoded or fluorescent.
results.quote: With this method, we achieved simultaneous recording from more than 300 spiking neurons within an 800-µm-diameter and 180-µm-thick volume in the mouse cortex, for more than 20 min.

results.finding: ASAP5-Kv recorded spikes from 9 mouse motor-cortex neurons in vivo at 450 frames per second.
results.detail: The neurons were sparsely labeled and recorded during locomotion. The example does not establish complete-population recording.
results.quote: In one example, we recorded from 9 neuronal cell bodies distributed across −85 μm to −278 μm in depth at 450 fps, observing contrasting relationships between locomotion and firing rates in individual neurons across long time scales (

results.finding: ASAP3-Kv detected 122 of 143 action potentials in one patch-clamped neuron in a study of 8 neurons in 3 mice.
results.detail: The paired recordings were made in anesthetized mice. Seven neurons fired 1,022 spikes; one had sufficient spike discriminability for the reported algorithmic detection rate. The study did not establish complete-population recording.
results.quote: AP detection by MLspike yielded a true-positive rate of 82.5% (122 out of 143 APs) with a false-positive rate of only 5.6%
